2016_088_011916mtg.paragraph: Agenda packet for the Troy Board of Education's organizational and regular meeting of January 19, 2016 at the Services Building. The organizational half elects officers and re-designates the treasurer, depositories, counsel and meeting schedule. The regular half honors Troy High students who raised over $31,500 for a classmate with Non-Hodgkins Lymphoma, appoints David Pass Director of Employee Services from a field of more than fifty applicants, receives the district's first M-STEP results showing Troy ranked #1 in Oakland County on combined ELA and mathematics, and approves a memorandum of understanding with Beijing Weiming Education Group bringing ten Chinese students to Troy for their senior year.
2016_088_011916mtg.page:
**Meeting**
Organizational and regular meeting, January 19, 2016, 7:00 PM, Services Building, 4420 Livernois.

**The organizational half**
The familiar sequence: elect an acting chairperson to officiate until a president is elected, appoint a temporary secretary, then elect president, vice president and secretary; appoint the treasurer; establish fund depositories and the investment resolution; designate board and district legal counsel; designate the superintendent deputy secretary; designate a person for posting notices; and adopt the meeting schedule for the 2016 calendar year.

**Recognition — "Caring for Karen"**
The Board recognizes Troy High students and staff "who came together to raise money for a fellow student battling a life-threatening disease." The school-wide effort was spearheaded by **Harriet Clark's Personal Communication classes and Troy High's Student Government**, and raised **over $31,500 for the Karen Barrientos Cancer fund** — Karen being an 11th grade student at Troy High with Non-Hodgkins Lymphoma. Principal Remo Roncone describes the effort; participants shake hands with the Board and a folder of certificates goes to the teacher for distribution. Dozens of students are named, among them Noor Al-Sharabi, Julia Alaimo, Katie Armstrong, Demiana Attalla, Victoria Bennett, Frenscheska Brikho, Savannah Cavendar-Le Mieux and Eric Cheng.

The first recognition item is Board Recognition Month.

**Consent agenda**
Minutes of the December 1, 2015 special meeting and workshop, the December 15, 2015 meeting, and the November 2015 Treasurer's Report.

**Treasurer's Report — November 2015**
Total check disbursements are $5,375,669.60, the General Fund group $3,477,732.82 and the General Fund (101) itself $3,172,152.99. Adding $1,962,353.96 of wire transfers, $157,790.88 of P-Card purchases and $17,422.93 of ACH debits, less $1,983.19 of prior period voids, total disbursements in period are $7,511,254.18.

**Personnel — Director of Employee Services**
**David Pass** is appointed. He has served as principal of Troy Union Elementary for the past four years and was asked to serve as Interim Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction during Kris Griffor's absence. Before Troy he was assistant principal at Avondale Middle School and elementary principal at R. Grant Graham Elementary in Avondale. He holds a degree in elementary education and a graduate degree in curriculum, instruction and leadership from Oakland University, and was then enrolled in the Education Specialist program at the University of Michigan with an anticipated April 2016 graduation.

Unlike the 2017 appointments, the packet publishes the **full applicant list rather than a funnel** — more than fifty names including Gregory Hampton, Brenda Guinan, Sonya Byrd, Virginia Krolczyk, Melissa Daugherty, Renee Klimkowski, Claude Tiller Jr, Reid Perry, Keichea Shauntee-Wilson, Donald Neibert, Joan Newberry, Walter Stevenson Jr., Jay Arnold, Shannon Carrico, Thomas Harrell, Sherry Morton, James Mallett, Carlita Earl, Shawn Shivnen, Rachel Turner, Lisa Kakos, Michael Grant, Brian Bedard and Kellie Cunningham. (Pass would appear a year later on the Board's TEA negotiating team.)

**Curriculum — the first M-STEP results**
Mark Dziatczak reports the district's spring 2015 M-STEP results with an Oakland County comparison. M-STEP tested ELA in grades 3-8 and 11, mathematics in grades 3-8 and 11, science in grades 4, 7 and 11, and social studies in grades 5, 8 and 11.

Troy's county rankings, combined and then grade by grade:

| Subject | Combined | By grade |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ELA (3-8, 11) | **#1** | #1 #1 #1 #1 #1 #2 #1 |
| Mathematics (3-8, 11) | **#1** | #3 #1 #2 #1 #1 #4 #1 |
| Science (4, 7, 11) | #7 | #11 #11 #2 |
| Social Studies (5, 8, 11) | #2 | #1 #5 #4 |

By subgroup, Troy ranks **#2 in ELA and #1 in mathematics for special education students**, and #2 in ELA for economically disadvantaged students. The report's conclusions note that **test standards — the cut scores for proficiency levels — increased for 2015**, the first year of the new assessment.

The science result is the outlier: #11 in the county at both grade 4 and grade 7 against #1 or #2 nearly everywhere else. It is the same relative weakness the 2018 gap analysis would still be tracking.

**Curriculum — the Weiming pilot**
Mark Dziatczak has negotiated a Memorandum of Understanding with **Beijing Weiming Education Group** for a Chinese and American student exchange. Eligible Chinese students would take part in a **three-plus-one year program** — three years at Weiming schools in China, then transferring to Troy for one year. Troy students would have the opportunity to study at a Weiming high school for summer or winter camps or as exchange students.

The stated goal is to encourage international education for Chinese and American students, teachers and administrators "in order to create a greater understanding between the two cultures, thus preparing students for a global economy," and the item notes the program aligns with **recent Oakland County initiatives designed to establish economic partnerships in China**. The resolution approves the MOU and provides that in the first year of the pilot, **a limited number of ten Chinese foreign students will spend their senior year enrolled in the Troy School District**.

**Other**
Board Vice-President Mr. Schmidt is approved to attend the NSBA Advocacy Institute, under Board Policy B-2001, Workshops and Conferences — the earlier policy numbering, before the district renumbered it 1000.01.

Agenda packet for the organizational and regular meeting of the Troy School District Board of Education, January 19, 2016, 7:00 PM at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. The agenda is: 1. Pledge of Allegiance; 2. Election of Acting Chairperson; 3. Appointment of Temporary Secretary; 4. Annual Organizational Meeting of the Board of Education — A. Nomination and Election of Officers (President, Vice President, Secretary), B. Appointment of Treasurer, C. Establish Fund Depositories and Investment Resolution for 2015/16 and 2016/17, D. Designation of Board and District Legal Counsel, E. Designation of Superintendent to be Deputy Secretary, F. Designation of a Person for Posting Notices of Meetings, G. Meeting Schedule for 2016 Calendar Year; 5. Recognition — A. Board Recognition Month, B. TSD Mission Moment: Troy High Students' "Caring for Karen" Fundraising Efforts; 6. Additions & Deletions; 7. Public Communication (agenda items); 8. General – Consent Agenda — A. Minutes of the December 1, 2015 Special Board of Education Meeting, B. Minutes of the December 1, 2015 Board of Education Workshop, C. Minutes of the December 15, 2015 Board of Education Meeting, D. Treasurer's Report – November 2015; 9. Personnel — A. Consideration: Elementary and Secondary, B. Consideration: Administrative Appointment – Director, Employee Services; 10. Curriculum — A. M-Step Results & County Comparison, B. Weiming International Student Pilot; 11. Business; 12. Public Communication (non-agenda items); 13. Other — A. 2016 NSBA Advocacy Conference; 14. Adjournment. Meetings are cablecast on TS-TV Channel 19 (Comcast) and Channel 15 (WOW) every Monday and Wednesday at 2:00 and 9:00 p.m. when school is in session, and viewable at http://vimeo.com/troyschools. (The two curriculum items carry the section header "10. BUSINESS" on their item pages while the agenda index lists section 10 as Curriculum.)

**The agenda memo and organizational items.** Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D. writes to the Board setting out the organizational sequence, beginning with the election of an acting chairperson who will conduct the meeting until a president has been elected. The organizational items follow the pattern used in the 2017 packet: nomination and election of president, vice president and secretary in turn; appointment of the school board treasurer; establishment of fund depositories and the investment resolution for 2015/16 and 2016/17; designation of board and district legal counsel; designation of the superintendent to be deputy secretary; designation of a person for posting notices of meetings; and adoption of the meeting schedule for the 2016 calendar year.

**Recognition 5.A: Board Recognition Month.** The annual January item recognizing the work of the Board of Education.

**Recognition 5.B: "Caring for Karen."** The Board recognizes a special group of Troy High students and staff who came together to raise money for a fellow student battling a life-threatening disease. The item records pride in "the all-out school wide effort spearheaded by Harriet Clark's Personal Communication classes and Troy High's Student Government," which raised over $31,500 for the Karen Barrientos Cancer fund. Karen is an 11th grade student at Troy High with Non-Hodgkins Lymphoma.

Mr. Remo Roncone, Troy High's principal, is invited to describe the efforts, after which the staff and students who organized the projects come up to receive recognition. The staging is specified: participants shake hands with the Board, and a folder containing all the certificates is presented to the teacher or administrator for distribution to individuals — a practical accommodation for a group too large to hand certificates to one by one. The students named include Noor Al-Sharabi, Julia Alaimo, Katie Armstrong, Demiana Attalla, Victoria Bennett, Frenscheska Brikho, Savannah Cavendar-Le Mieux and Eric Cheng, among many others.

Harriet Clark, who taught the Personal Communication classes that led the effort, appears again in the April 2017 packet among the 35 Outstanding Teacher nominees, listed as teaching communications, debate and English at Troy High.

**Consent agenda.** Minutes of the December 1, 2015 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the December 1, 2015 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the December 15, 2015 Board of Education Meeting; and the Treasurer's Report for November 2015.

**Treasurer's Report, November 2015.** General Fund (101) check disbursements are $3,172,152.99, with Total General Fund of $3,477,732.82 and TOTAL CHECK DISBURSEMENTS of $5,375,669.60. Adding ACH debits of $17,422.93, outgoing wire transfers of $1,962,353.96 and P-Card purchases of $157,790.88, and subtracting prior period void disbursements of $1,983.19, TOTAL DISBURSEMENTS IN PERIOD is $7,511,254.18. The middle sections of the packet are the November check register run by fund. The totals here run materially below the equivalent months in the 2017 and 2018 packets, which is what one would expect a year before the 2016 bond program began spending.

**Personnel 9.A: elementary and secondary.** The routine personnel recommendations item.

**Personnel 9.B: Director of Employee Services.** The recommendation is Mr. David Pass. He has served as principal of Troy Union Elementary School for the past four years, and was additionally asked to serve as Interim Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction during Kris Griffor's absence. Prior to coming to Troy he held several positions including assistant principal at Avondale Middle School and elementary principal at R. Grant Graham Elementary in Avondale. He holds a degree in elementary education from Oakland University and a graduate degree in curriculum, instruction and leadership from Oakland University, and is currently enrolled in the Education Specialist program at the University of Michigan with an anticipated graduation date of April 2016. The resolution approves his employment as Director of Employee Services without tenure in the administrative position.

The packet's treatment of the search differs from the practice the district would adopt a year later. Rather than the staged funnel published for the 2017 and 2018 appointments — applications received, first-round interviews, finalists, final selection — this packet simply prints a list headed "Troy School District Applicants for Employee Services" naming more than fifty people: Gregory Hampton, Brenda Guinan, Sonya Byrd, Virginia Krolczyk, Melissa Daugherty, Renee Klimkowski, Claude Tiller Jr, Reid Perry, Keichea Shauntee-Wilson, Donald Neibert, Joan Newberry, Walter Stevenson Jr., Jay Arnold, Shannon Carrico, Thomas Harrell, Sherry Morton, James Mallett, Carlita Earl, Shawn Shivnen, Rachel Turner, Lisa Kakos, Michael Grant, Brian Bedard, Kellie Cunningham and others. Every applicant is named in a public document, with no indication of who was interviewed — a more exposing disclosure than the later funnels, which name only those who reached an interview.

David Pass appears again in the February 2017 packet as a member of the Board's negotiating team for the TEA contract talks, alongside Jordan Harris as chief spokesperson.

**Curriculum 10.A: 2015 M-STEP results and county comparison.** Mark Dziatczak, Deputy Superintendent of Teaching and Learning, provides the district results of the spring 2015 M-STEP testing along with a comparison of scores with other Oakland County school districts. The presentation is dated January 12, 2016.

M-STEP in spring 2015 tested English language arts in grades 3-8 and 11; mathematics in grades 3-8 and 11; science in grades 4, 7 and 11; and social studies in grades 5, 8 and 11.

The presentation reports Troy's rank among Oakland County districts for each subject, first combined across grades and then grade by grade. In ELA across grades 3-8 and 11 combined, Troy ranks #1; by grade the ranks run #1, #1, #1, #1, #1, #2 and #1. In mathematics combined, Troy ranks #1; by grade the ranks run #3, #1, #2, #1, #1, #4 and #1. In science across grades 4, 7 and 11 combined, Troy ranks #7; by grade, #11, #11 and #2. In social studies across grades 5, 8 and 11 combined, Troy ranks #2; by grade, #1, #5 and #4.

Two subgroup breakdowns follow. For special education students, Troy ranks #2 in ELA across grades 3-8 and 11 combined and #1 in mathematics. For economically disadvantaged students, Troy ranks #2 in ELA combined.

The conclusions note that test standards — the cut scores that define proficiency levels — increased for 2015. This was M-STEP's first administration, replacing the MEAP, and the higher cut scores meant proficiency rates statewide fell sharply from the prior assessment; the county-rank framing the presentation uses sidesteps that discontinuity by comparing Troy against its peers on the same new test rather than against its own prior-year numbers.

The science result is the one clear weakness in an otherwise dominant showing: #11 in the county at grade 4 and again at grade 7, against #1 or #2 almost everywhere else, recovering to #2 by grade 11. The same relative pattern persists into the 2018 gap analysis, where science remains the subject on which Troy's margin over the county and state is narrowest.

**Curriculum 10.B: Weiming international student pilot.** Mark Dziatczak has negotiated a Memorandum of Understanding between the Troy School District and Weiming Education Group, outlining a Chinese and American student exchange program between Beijing Weiming Education Group and the district.

The MOU outlines the opportunity for eligible Chinese students from Weiming Education Group — referred to as Chinese Foreign Students — to participate in a three-plus-one year program, in which they study for three years at Weiming schools in China and subsequently transfer to the Troy School District for one year. Students from the Troy School District would also have the opportunity to study at one of Weiming's high schools for summer and winter camps and/or as exchange students.

The stated goal is to encourage international education for Chinese and American students, teachers and administrators in order to create a greater understanding between the two cultures, thus preparing students for a global economy. The item further notes that the program is aligned to recent Oakland County initiatives designed to establish economic partnerships in China and to promote opportunities for Oakland County businesses and ventures in China — an unusual justification for a curriculum item, tying a student exchange to county economic development policy.

The resolution approves the Memorandum of Understanding under the terms of the agreement and provides that in the first year of this pilot program, a limited number of ten Chinese foreign students will spend their senior year enrolled as students in the Troy School District.

The structure is worth noting for what it is and is not. It is not a Schools of Choice arrangement — those resolutions, adopted every February under Sections 105 and 105c, govern nonresident Michigan students and turn on which intermediate school district the applicant's home district sits in. This is a separate instrument entirely, admitting foreign nationals for a single senior year under a negotiated MOU, capped at ten students in the pilot year.

**Other 13.A: 2016 NSBA Advocacy Institute Conference attendance.** As required by Board Policy B-2001, Workshops and Conferences, expenditure of district funds for members for out-of-state meetings must have prior approval by resolution. Board Vice-President Mr. Schmidt has indicated his desire to attend the National School Boards Association Advocacy Institute Conference.

The policy citation is itself a small marker of time: by May 2017 the same requirement is cited as Board Policy 1000.01, Organization and Functioning of the Board; Reimbursement of Expenses, following the policy renumbering the Board adopted in December 2016 when it approved the revised Board of Education Bylaws and Policies.

Read as a whole, the January 2016 packet is the district at a quieter moment than the years that follow — no bond program yet spending, monthly disbursements running at half what they would reach by 2018, and an organizational meeting with no change in the Board's composition. What it does contain is a district looking outward in two directions at once: a first set of M-STEP results establishing Troy at or near the top of all Oakland County districts in ELA and mathematics, and a memorandum of understanding with a Beijing education group that would bring ten Chinese seniors into Troy High classrooms, justified partly by Oakland County's own economic ambitions in China. Between them sits a fundraiser in which one high school's communication classes and student government raised over $31,500 for a classmate with cancer.
